questions: Must the subgraph be induced (i.e., contain all edges of T between its selected vertices) or can we arbitrarily choose a subset of edges among the selected vertices?
When selecting a subgraph, are isolated vertices (degree 0) allowed, or must every chosen vertex have degree 1 or 4 within the subgraph?
If the subgraph contains vertices of degree 4, must those four incident edges all belong to the original tree T, or can we add edges not present in T?
Are we allowed to reuse vertices or edges of T in multiple candidate subgraphs, or must each vertex/edge be used at most once in the final selection?
Should the output be -1 only when no subgraph with at least one vertex satisfies the alkane conditions, or also when the only possible alkane subgraph consists of a single vertex of degree 1?
In the case of multiple maximal‑size alkanes, does the problem require any particular one to be output (e.g., lexicographically smallest vertex set), or is only the size needed?
Are there any constraints on N = 1 (a single‑vertex tree); does a single vertex count as an alkane if its degree is 0, or must the answer be -1?
Must the algorithm run within the given constraints (e.g., O(N) time), or are there hidden limits on memory or recursion depth that need clarification?
answers: Not specified beyond what's given; assume the subgraph must be induced, i.e. contain all edges of T between the selected vertices.
Not specified beyond what's given; every selected vertex must have degree exactly 1 or 4 within the subgraph, so isolated vertices are not allowed.
Yes, the four incident edges of a degree-4 vertex in the subgraph must all be edges present in the original tree T.
Not applicable; the question of 'reusing' vertices/edges across candidates doesn't apply since we're choosing a single subgraph.
The output should be -1 whenever no valid alkane subgraph -- one containing at least one degree-4 vertex -- exists; a subgraph with only degree-1 vertices does not qualify.
Not specified beyond what's given; only the size of the largest alkane subgraph is needed, not which one.
For N=1, a single vertex has degree 0, which doesn't satisfy 'degree 1 or 4' nor include a degree-4 vertex, so the answer would be -1.
Not specified beyond what's given; assume standard efficient algorithms are expected given the constraint size.
inline_prompts: You are given an undirected tree T with N vertices, numbered 1, 2, \ldots, N. The i-th edge is an undirected edge connecting vertices A_i and B_i. A graph is defined to be an alkane if and only if it satisfies the following conditions: - The graph is an undirected tree. - Every vertex has degree 1 or 4. Determine whether there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, and if so, find the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 B_1 A_2 B_2 \vdots A_{N - 1} B_{N - 1} Output If there exists a subgraph of T that is an alkane, print the maximum number of vertices in such a subgraph. Otherwise, print -1. Constraints - 1 \leq N \leq 2 \times 10^5 - 1 \leq A_i, B_i \leq N - The given graph is an undirected tree. - All input values are integers.
